claims.text: Conventional fabrication methods such as spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying typically produce W–Cu composites with interfacial voids, phase separation, and nonuniform W–Cu contacts.
A nanometer-scale copper coating can be deposited conformally on tungsten particles by atomic layer deposition before consolidation.
The pre-deposited copper interlayer will enhance sintering contact between tungsten surfaces and the copper matrix.
Copper pre-coating will improve the wettability of tungsten during sintering.
Copper pre-coating will increase interfacial atomic diffusion during sintering.
Improved wettability and interfacial diffusion will reduce interfacial void formation.
Improved wettability and interfacial diffusion will reduce phase separation during consolidation.
Copper pre-coating will promote more uniform interparticle contact in the consolidated W–Cu composite.
Reduced defects and more uniform W–Cu contact will improve thermal transport.
The ALD-pre-coated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise identically spark-plasma-sintered composite without pre-coating.
The ALD-pre-coated composite will have fewer interfacial voids than the uncoated spark-plasma-sintered baseline.
The improved interface will preserve mechanical durability under cyclic fusion-relevant irradiation conditions.
The ALD-pre-coated composite will show improved mechanical performance under simulated fusion-relevant conditions relative to the uncoated baseline.
The proposed service boundary extends to approximately 500 °C.
The proposed evaluation includes fusion-relevant irradiation and thermal cycling to approximately 500 °C.
Interactions between the ALD layer and sintering dynamics may affect the magnitude of the thermal and mechanical improvements.
Irradiation-induced microstructural changes may alter the predicted outcome.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis requires mechanical durability to be preserved, whereas the predicted outcome and falsification rule require a statistically significant improvement in mechanical performance. Preservation and improvement are different success criteria.

The falsification rule treats lack of improvement in thermal conductivity and mechanical durability as equivalent to comparable or worse defect density and interparticle contact, but these structural and performance outcomes are not logically equivalent and could diverge.
